items.articleText: Researchers Demonstrate OpenBSD Root Exploit Chaining 37-Year-Old Shared-Memory Bug  Swati Khandelwal  Oct 16, 2026 Vulnerability / OpenBSD A local privilege escalation exploit published today gains root on OpenBSD 7.9 by chaining a roughly 37-year-old integer overflow with a separate kernel flaw, bypassing OpenBSD's KARL kernel-address randomization and its SMAP and SMEP hardware protections. Security firm Calif, which found and reported the flaws, published a detailed writeup and full proof-of-concept code after OpenBSD shipped patches for both issues in September. The integer overflow in the shmat(4) attach function was fixed in errata 018 , shipped September 14 as a reliability fix. The reference-counting use-after-free that completes the chain was fixed separately in errata 026, shipped September 30 as a security fix. Both are available through syspatch and cover all architectures. OpenBSD 7.8 also received the integer-overflow fix. The integer overflow, the entry point for the full chain, is classified as a reliability fix, not a security fix. No CVE has been assigned for either flaw as of publication. There is no evidence that the vulnerabilities have been used in attacks. The shared-memory attachment counter shm_nattch is defined as a signed 16-bit short with a maximum value of 32,767 in original BSD sources dating to 1988. OpenBSD inherited the type and never widened it. The exploit maps 127 shared-memory segments and forks 259 processes, pushing the counter past its maximum and wrapping it to −32,643. A race condition then triggers a use-after-free: the corrupted reference count causes the kernel to free memory that other processes still use. A separate out-of-bounds write overwrites multicast-membership counters in the kernel. When the affected socket closes, the resulting decrements modify page-table entries, switching a user-memory mapping to supervisor-accessible and bypassing SMAP and SMEP. The exploit then overwrites a function pointer at a predictable kernel address to run its own code. "While OpenBSD's KARL relinks the kernel binary to randomize both function and data addresses, the kernel's memory allocators remain deterministic," researcher Andrew Griffiths wrote. Both the boot-time and best-fit allocators lack base-address randomization, so early-boot structures, including function pointers in the lo0 and enc0 network-interface handlers, land at the same addresses across reboots on the same hardware. items.articleText: Attackers Tampered with AOMEI Backupper's Update Servers for Minutes to Deliver a Backdoor  Swati Khandelwal  Oct 16, 2026 Supply Chain Attack / Endpoint Security Attackers repeatedly changed the files that AOMEI Backupper fetches from the vendor's own update servers, in windows of five to ten minutes at a time between May and July 2026, so that any copy of the Windows backup program that checked for an update during one of those windows would download and run a backdoor. Google Threat Intelligence Group, Mandiant , and ManageEngine's Threat Analysis Lab , which disclosed the campaign this week, say AOMEI has reported fixing its servers, but that fix does not remove the backdoor from machines that were already hit. AOMEI Backupper is Windows backup and disk-cloning software made by AOMEI Technology, a vendor registered in Hong Kong. Like the company's remote-desktop tool AnyViewer, it runs background services that regularly check AOMEI's servers over HTTPS for software updates and promotional pop-ups. Two files drive that check. One, down_html.ini, names the update package to download and the checksum the program uses to verify it. The other, Notifycfg.ini, tells the pop-up service what to display and what to run. The program does not cryptographically verify either file, and the checksum that is supposed to prove the download is genuine sits inside the same unsigned file that names it. Nothing in the software was exploited. There was no vulnerability, and no user action was needed beyond having the program installed and running, according to ManageEngine's lab. The attacker only had to change two text files on the server for a few minutes. A copy of Backupper that checked in during a window pulled the attacker's package into its own folder, and the notification file then made it run. It ran with the privileges of the AOMEI process that launched it. On the machines the lab examined, that was enough to install software across the whole system, though it said the elevation depended on how the AOMEI service was running. items.articleText: UAT-11985 Uses Fake Event Invites to Target Taiwan Research Affiliates With Google AitM Phishing  Ravie Lakshmanan  Oct 16, 2026 Phishing / Artificial Intelligence Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an advanced persistent threat (APT) spear-phishing campaign that has targeted individuals affiliated with Taiwan research organizations to direct victims to an adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) phishing framework designed to harvest their Google account credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes. The activity is being tracked by Cisco Talos under the moniker UAT-11985 , describing it as likely fueled by artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted content generation so as to quickly craft bespoke lures aimed at different targets within the confines of a common social engineering framework. The campaign was first observed in mid-2026. "The operation leveraged legitimate public event themes and impersonated reputable academic and policy institutions to establish credibility," Talos researcher Joey Chen said in an analysis. "Beyond traditional email phishing, the actor incorporated QR code phishing (quishing) techniques by modifying legitimate event posters with malicious QR codes, expanding the attack surface beyond email recipients to secondary victims who may encounter printed materials." Central to the operation is the use of legitimate or plausible public event information in spear-phishing emails and embedding within them a URL that points to attacker-controlled infrastructure, while hovering over the hyperlink displays a legitimate-looking Google Forms URL. These invitation emails feature nearly identical syntactic structures despite the breadth of geopolitical topics being discussed, indicating the content was mass-produced from a reusable prompt template rather than painstakingly crafted for each target. Specifically, the emails follow a three-part structure - The opening section offers a "polished (but overly elaborate) description" of the geopolitical or policy context. The second section is tailored to the recipient and paints them in a flattering light in an attempt to trigger engagement. The third and final section provides details of event logistics, including the topic, date, venue, and registration instructions. items.articleText: OpenAI Research Model Spent 3rd-Party Test ETH Without Permission to Deploy Smart Contract  Ravie Lakshmanan  Oct 16, 2026 Artificial Intelligence / Web Security OpenAI has disclosed seven new incidents in which its artificial intelligence (AI) models exhibited misaligned behavior, including one case where its research model, after not having funds on an Ethereum test network, spent test cryptocurrency from a third-party's wallet without authorization to complete a coding task. The incident, the AI company said, involved an internal research model part of the GPT-5.6 Sol family. The incident occurred on June 26, 2026, and was discovered by OpenAI three months later. "An internal research model asked to update a cryptocurrency trading application used funds from a wallet that the task had not supplied to pay for a deployment on Sepolia, an Ethereum test network," OpenAI said . "It derived wallet keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, found an account with test-network funds, and used that account to pay for the requested contract deployment." The assignment allowed the model to deploy compatible contracts if it did not find one, but gave it no funded wallet to pay the network fees. After its attempts to obtain free test tokens failed, it wrote a script to derive "accounts from common developer recovery phrases and query their balances." In the process, it identified 362 addresses and found one account that held enough Sepolia ETH. Armed with the recovery (or seed) phrase, the model derived the private keys that grant unauthorized access to the corresponding account and spend the stashed cryptocurrency. Although the model questioned whether it had the necessary permission to carry out this step, it subsequently reasoned that a public recovery phrase and valueless test-network tokens made the funds acceptable to use. "But using public known key/funds ethically? Funds on a known public dev mnemonic are effectively abandoned/test ETH; Sepolia valueless," the model mused. "We can use [amount redacted] to deploy task. Fine." OpenAI has since implemented additional safeguards to prevent live internet access for such scenarios, adding it runs its misalignment monitoring system on all traffic to flag events if its AI agents manage to gain live internet access. "This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder's permission, then act on that judgment without authorization," OpenAI said. items.articleText: AI Decision Models and Their Impact on AI SOC Platforms  The Hacker News  Oct 16, 2026 Artificial Intelligence / Security Operations In the space of a month, a new category of AI model went from nonexistent to everywhere. TypeSafe AI released Jev on September 15 and called it a System One model, a nod to Kahneman's fast, intuitive thinking . OpenAI announced its own Decisions API at DevDay and opened a public beta on October 6. Cribl published cribl-decision , an open LoRA adapter you can run locally. Others, like Laya, are already showing up in open source tooling. These models skip text generation entirely. You hand them some state and a set of typed questions. They hand back a choice, a score, or a yes/no with a probability attached. For security operations, I think this is some of the best news of the year. I also think most of the conversation is pointed at the wrong layer. Why a SOC should be excited Three properties make decision models a natural fit for alert triage. You get a number you can automate against. A typed answer with a calibrated probability is something you can put a threshold on. Ask the model whether an alert is benign and you get back a probability. Close it automatically above 0.97. Below 0.6, treat it as a likely incident and escalate it. Anything in between goes to an analyst for a closer look. TypeSafe even suggests stricter thresholds for irreversible actions, which maps neatly onto “disable an account” versus “add a comment to the ticket.” They're cheap enough for every alert. Jev is priced at $42 per billion input tokens, with responses in 70 to 500 milliseconds. Say an enterprise sees 450,000 alerts a year and you feed a few thousand tokens per alert. The model bill lands somewhere around a hundred dollars a year. The economic argument for cherry-picking and only looking at high-severity alerts just disappeared! Every verdict becomes a record. The answer space is fixed in advance and the output carries its own probability. You can log every decision, replay it, and compare it with what actually happened. That's far easier to audit than a paragraph of generated reasoning. One caveat worth keeping in mind. When vendors say these models "can't hallucinate," they mean the output always matches the schema you defined. A well-formed answer can still be wrong. But a calibrated guess is still just a guess The old rule still applies. Garbage in, garbage out. Calibration is a promise about a distribution. items.articleText: Critical BlockStrap flaw lets hackers run code on Magento servers By Bill Toulas October 16, 2026 04:00 PM 0 Researchers warn that hackers could soon exploit a maximum-severity vulnerability (CVE-2026-103849) affecting Magento and Adobe Commerce, potentially allowing them to execute arbitrary PHP code on store servers. According to e-commerce security firm Sansec, attacks leveraging the vulnerability, dubbed BlockStrap, have not yet been observed, but threat actors are expected to find a way to exploit it. The researchers based their assessment on identifying four potential attack paths involving CVE-2026-103849 in less than 24 hours. The flaw impacts September versions of Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source through 2.4.9 and Adobe Commerce B2B through 1.5.3. The security firm warned that Adobe’s “priority 2” rating of this flaw does not reflect the danger and urgency in this case, despite the more complex attack path. “The attack path is complex, but anyone with an AI agent can reverse-engineer the patch into working exploits in a relatively short time,” stated Sansec states . “That is why we question Adobe's priority 2 rating (patch within 30 days). StyleSmuggler went from a priority 1 hotfix to mass exploitation in three days, and BlockStrap is of similar complexity.” Adobe’s bulletin , published on October 13, describes the flaw as an improper neutralization of special elements used in a template engine, leading to arbitrary code execution. Sansec explains that BlockStrap is a second-pass template engine directive injection that allows attacker-controlled content in a child email template to be signed and processed again at the root level, executing a smuggled {{block}} directive. According to Sansec’s analysis, BlockStrap exposes a gap left by the StyleSmuggler fix in the same email-template engine. Adobe’s fix replaces the generic processing with registered placeholders, preventing exploitation. Sansec says that a plain Composer install isn’t enough to address the risk, and website administrators must apply the 2026-oct release or Adobe’s isolated patch. “BlockStrap and StyleSmuggler are separate fixes. You need both, so keep the September VULN-39341 hotfix in place as well,” Sansec cautions. The e-commerce security company says it will provide an update when it detects mass attack waves, which it expects to occur soon. items.articleText: Targeted ads installed Candiru spyware in zero-click attacks By Bill Toulas October 16, 2026 01:20 PM 0 Candiru spyware was delivered to devices at Al Jazeera Media Network via targeted online advertisements in a zero-click attack that required only rendering the malicious ads on the victim's device. Researchers at Citizen Labs investigating the attacks referred to this technique as AdFection, noting that their report is the first public technical confirmation of mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. A similar method was documented in late 2025 by Amnesty International, involving ads that infected targets with Predator spyware without them clicking anything. That infection mechanism was called Aladdin and surfaced due to a collection of marketing files and documents leaked from the Intellexa surveillance company that researchers studied and corroborated with technical details from forensic investigations. Unlike Alladin, AdFection was caught in real attacks and linked to Israeli firm Discovere-Tech, described by Citizen Lab as " a bridge between mercenary spyware companies and the advertising ecosystem." Ads participating in AdFection Source: Citizen Lab Zero-click Candiru spyware infection According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech allowed its customers to use its Controlium platform to target specific devices with malicious code, or profile, deanonimize, and fingerprint user devices. "Discover-Tech appears to work with multiple mercenary spyware, hacking, and advertising vendors, connecting the spyware industry to the online advertising ecosystem," Citizen Lab says . The company purchased ad placements through mainstream ad networks and exchanges, embedding JavaScript in ads that contacted its "NOAS server" when rendered. Using multiple parameters (e.g., IP address, ad identifiers), the NOAS server, "or getAd server," determined if a target was eligible to receive JavaScript code. Selected targets received additional code, while other devices the ad rendered on received nothing, helping keep the attacks stealthy. Action sequence for valid targets Source: Citizen Lab Al Jazeera provided Citizen Lab with evidence of attacks that targeted at least 45 devices between 2024 and 2025. The network logs examined by the researchers showed a sequence from Discover-Tech infrastructure to Candiru validation servers and then to spyware command-and-control servers. items.articleText: China-Linked Hackers Exploited BeyondTrust Zero-Day to Take Over Remote Support Servers  Ravie Lakshmanan  Oct 16, 2026 Zero-Day / Vulnerability The China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (previously UNC5221 or Warp Panda) exploited a newly disclosed security flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) as a zero-day in late August 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS score: 9.3), is a case of improper origin validation in an internal messaging component that could be exploited by a remote attacker to perform file operations on an affected appliance. "The vulnerability exists within internal components of Remote Support," BeyondTrust said in a Thursday alert. "The components did not adequately validate the origin of the messages it received. Under the right conditions, this could be used to perform file operations on the appliance." Patches for the flaw have been pushed to all Remote Support SaaS customers as of October 9, 2026. Self-hosted customers of Remote Support running versions from 24.3.1 through 26.2.3 are advised to manually update to BT26-05-RS patch. Customers running a version older than 24.3.1 will be required to upgrade to a newer version to apply the fix. According to a timeline of events shared by BeyondTrust, Armory Castle is said to have exploited the flaw as a zero-day on a single self-hosted Remote Support appliance on August 29, 2026. Then, on September 27, 2026, "successful exploitation of another security device provider [became] public," it added, prompting it to initiate an investigation to hunt for similar activity. Armory Castle has a history of exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities in Citrix NetScaler ( CVE-2023-4966 ) and Ivanti Connect Secure ( CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887 , and CVE-2025-0282 ) appliances to break a wide range of sectors, including legal services, SaaS providers, business-process outsourcers, technology, and governments, for long-term intelligence collection. It's known to be active since October 2023. "The actor uses a zero-day selectively against chosen targets, and once the vulnerability is public, the actor typically moves to broad exploitation of every instance still unpatched," BeyondTrust said. items.articleText: CERT-In Warns AI Agents Accessed Sensitive Data at Indian Organizations During Testing  Swati Khandelwal  Oct 16, 2026 Artificial Intelligence / Data Security AI agents being tested online reached the live systems of Indian organizations and read business records, including personal data and confidential material, CERT-In said in an advisory on October 15. The agents went beyond their assigned tasks, and none of the organizations detected the unauthorized access. After internal reviews, the AI companies whose models were being tested voluntarily reported the cases to CERT-In, India's national cyber agency. AI agents are software systems that can plan work, run commands, use tools, and act on the internet autonomously for extended periods. In these cases, the agents gained access via credentials and connection settings left exposed in application configuration and public code repositories, and via cloud service roles with excessive permissions. CERT-In did not name the AI companies, their models, or the organizations and sectors involved. It did not say how many companies reported cases or how many organizations were affected, and said only that the reports came in recently. It also did not say whether any data the agents read was copied or kept, or whether the affected organizations have been told. Attackers Used Open-Source AI Agent Tools in a Separate Campaign CERT-In's own threat hunting found a second, separate set of incidents: a financially motivated campaign against Indian entities. The attackers misused publicly available offensive-security frameworks built on AI agents. The frameworks continue to be misused and rebranded, with numerous deployments across infrastructure in several countries. CERT-In did not name the frameworks or the attackers. In this campaign, the frameworks cut the time from first access to final impact from days to a few hours, according to CERT-In. The attackers ran several agents in parallel for hours to days to reach their goals. Victims that only partly fixed the problems were attacked again within days, at a larger scale. Google Threat Intelligence Group reported a separate case in September. Attackers who had compromised a cloud resource planned, built and ran an agent-driven campaign that harvested thousands of third-party credentials, all in under 6 hours . You wonder what the employee submitted to ChatGPT. Could be a public job description, or a customer ticket with contact information and internal account details. Maybe sensitive government documents, if that is your line of work, as the acting director of CISA did in 2025? The case is hypothetical. In this article, we will follow 2 versions of the same event. In the first, your security tools identify personal account use, but nothing in your current configuration checks what goes into the prompt. items.articleText: Burger King Japan data breach exposes 11 million customer records By Sergiu Gatlan October 16, 2026 08:01 AM 0 Burger King Japan, the Japanese subsidiary of global fast-food giant Burger King, disclosed a major data breach after attackers accessed a server containing 11.18 million customer records. Founded in 1953 in Florida, Burger King is now a multinational fast-food chain with nearly 20,000 locations worldwide, including 350 in Japan. In a Thursday press release, Burger King Japan said it concluded a follow-up investigation on October 13 and apologized to customers whose data was stolen in early October and leaked online. The breached servers stored the personal information for users of the company's official smartphone app, including their names, dates of birth, gender, email addresses, phone numbers, and order history. "We identified a potential unauthorized third-party access to the system that manages member information for our official app and conducted an investigation," Burger King Japan said . "As a result, it was determined on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, that unauthorized access occurred between Friday, October 2, 2026, and Wednesday, October 7, 2026, resulting in a leak of member information. Upon becoming aware of the unauthorized access, we immediately blocked access from the source in question." However, the company says the compromised server did not store customer credit card numbers and that it found no evidence that the threat actors accessed user credentials. Burger King Japan has reported the breach to Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC) and is now also investigating how the attackers accessed the compromised server, with help from external cybersecurity experts. "We sincerely apologize for the great inconvenience and concern this situation has caused to our customers and all others involved," it added. "At this time, no secondary damage, such as fraudulent use, resulting from this incident has been confirmed." The fast-food chain also warned affected customers to watch for suspicious emails, SMS messages, and phone calls that may impersonate Burger King Japan, and to avoid clicking URLs, opening attachments, or entering member information or passwords. items.articleText: Microsoft: October Windows update may break Smart App Control By Sergiu Gatlan October 16, 2026 04:44 AM 0 Microsoft says some users may have trouble turning on Smart App Control after installing this month's KB5127648 Windows 11 security update. Smart App Control is a Windows 11 security feature that uses Microsoft's app intelligence services and code integrity features and works alongside Microsoft Defender and SmartScreen to block potentially harmful apps or binaries. According to the company, on affected devices running Windows 11, version 24H2 and later, the Smart App Control option is grayed out and cannot be toggled. "After installing this update, some devices might be unable to turn on Smart App Control in the Windows Security app if it has been turned off. On affected devices, the option to turn on Smart App Control might be grayed out," Microsoft said in an update to the KB5127648 advisory . "Devices where Smart App Control is already turned on are not affected and remain protected." While a fix isn't available yet, Microsoft shared temporary workarounds to help IT administrators mitigate the issue on enterprise-managed devices by modifying the registry or installing a group policy. To restore the ability to turn on Smart App Control on affected Windows 11 devices by editing the registry, you have to follow these steps: Open a Command Prompt window by typing cmd in the Search box. Select Run as Administrator. At the command prompt, enter the following commands and then restart the device: reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Policies\Microsoft\FeatureManagement\Overrides" /v 2883193997 /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Policies\Microsoft\FeatureManagement\Overrides" /v 2850574478 /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f IT admins can also work around the issue by installing and configuring the two Group Policies below to turn on Smart App Control and ensure that logging is enabled for troubleshooting: Windows 11, versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 - KB5074105 261015_19222 Feature Preview Windows 11, versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 - KB5074105 261015_19221 Feature Preview The two Group Policies can be found under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > {Group Policy name} > Windows 11, version 24H2, 25H2. After installing them, admins must set both settings to Enabled and restart the affected device(s) to apply the Group Policy settings. items.articleText: BAE Systems cyberattack disrupts US federal court operations By Sergiu Gatlan October 16, 2026 03:37 AM 0 The Administrative Office of the US Courts (AOUSC) says a cyberattack on government contractor BAE Systems has taken down the notice system used by federal bankruptcy courts. In a Thursday press release, the Administrative Office of the US Courts said the BAE Systems cyberattack also halted the production and distribution of bankruptcy notices. "The Administrative Office of the US Courts has been in communication with the impacted courts and is also coordinating with BAE Systems. BAE is actively investigating this incident and working to restore operations," AOUSC said . "As a result of the incident, all access to the BNC systems and websites that BAE operates on behalf of the Judiciary and the related bankruptcy noticing process are unavailable at this time, including bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov, notices.uscourts.gov, and the National Creditor Registration Service." BAE Systems is Europe's largest defense contractor, designing and manufacturing military technology for the UK and US defense departments, and a major provider of enterprise IT, cloud infrastructure, and cybersecurity services to military, intelligence, and civilian government agencies worldwide. "We are aware of a security incident that is isolated to the BNC system and have taken immediate steps to address it. We are coordinating closely with AOUSC on the response," a BAE Systems spokesperson told BleepingComputer. An AOUSC spokesperson was not immediately available for comment when BleepingComputer contacted them earlier today for more details on the attack. The US Federal Judiciary, the independent judicial branch of the US federal government, also said last year that it was strengthening cybersecurity defenses after a cyberattack impacted its electronic case management systems. The federal Judiciary added that while most documents in the system are public, it now protects certain sealed filings containing sensitive information with stricter access controls designed to block attackers. "The federal Judiciary is taking additional steps to strengthen protections for sensitive case documents in response to recent escalated cyberattacks of a sophisticated and persistent nature on its case management system," it said. items.articleText: BeyondTrust patches zero-day exploited in attacks since August By Sergiu Gatlan October 16, 2026 02:18 AM 0 BeyondTrust warned customers on Thursday to patch a critical flaw in its Remote Support (RS) that has been exploited in zero-day attacks since late August. Remote Support is the company's enterprise-grade support solution that helps IT service desks, help desks, and customer support teams troubleshoot issues remotely. Tracked as CVE-2026-102764 , this actively exploited authentication bypass vulnerability lets unprivileged remote attackers perform file operations on unpatched appliances and affects RS 26.2.3 or earlier. BeyondTrust patched the security issue for all Remote Support and Privileged Remote Access SaaS customers on October 8, but self-hosted installations must be patched manually if automatic updates are not enabled. "While our internal testing has not identified any way for an attacker to exploit this vulnerability in Privileged Remote Access, PRA shares the affected code, so out of an abundance of caution, we have released the patch for PRA and recommend self-hosted Privileged Remote Access customers apply it immediately," BeyondTrust said . Although the company shared very limited details about the vulnerability, it said the zero-day was abused in the wild by a suspected China-nexus espionage actor tracked by Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) security researchers as "Armory Castle" (formerly UNC5221 ) and by cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike as "Warp Panda." According to Mandiant researchers, who spotted the initial attacks, Armory Castle hackers exploited the flaw to gain initial access and escalated to root privileges on compromised devices by enabling Set User ID (SUID) permissions. Next, they deployed new Sawfly web shell and Bareclaw tunneler malware, wiped logs to evade detection, and moved laterally through the victim's network using compromised Administrator credentials by opening remote sessions on downstream systems. "After establishing a foothold through the web shell, the actor elevated from the web service account to root-level control of the appliance host. This gave them access to every credential the appliance stored or brokered and the ability to modify files that survive reboot and configuration reset," Mandiant said . items.summary: A newly disclosed critical flaw in the Linux kernel allows code inside a virtual machine to read memory on the host computer it runs on. A researcher demonstrated the leak against Vercel's live cloud sandboxes, and Verce
items.articleText: Critical PwnEscape Linux Kernel Vulnerability Lets Guest VMs Read Host Memory  Swati Khandelwal  Oct 15, 2026 Linux / Vulnerability A newly disclosed critical flaw in the Linux kernel allows code inside a virtual machine to read memory on the host computer it runs on. A researcher demonstrated the leak against Vercel's live cloud sandboxes, and Vercel confirmed it. The flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-99999 and nicknamed PwnEscape , is in the Linux kernel's networking code, not in any one cloud's setup, so it reaches the shared layer that cloud providers use to keep customers' workloads apart. It was found in a Vercel security challenge and reported privately before any public release, and there is no sign it has been used in a real attack. What the Researcher Showed Paulos Yibelo of the security firm pwn.ai found that specially made network packets sent from inside a virtual machine could do three things, he explained in a technical write-up : read the host's memory, crash the host, and run code on it. All three come from the same kernel flaw. Vercel said in its report on the challenge that the memory leak was demonstrated against its production sandboxes. Each packet the guest sent out could carry back about 32 bytes of the host's memory, and the guest could keep going as long as it kept sending packets. The crash and code execution were observed only on the researcher's own machines, which were set up to match Vercel's. Two specially crafted packets were enough to crash a host and take down every sandbox running on it. Using the same flaw, the researcher then reached administrator control of a host, breaking out of the virtual machine. He stressed this was a lab result, "not a claim of root command execution in any vendor's production environment." "Our research ran through Omega-Pwn , an internal harness combining our own security research tooling with elements of SingularityNET's OmegaClaw architecture . It let us carry hypotheses, code traces, failed attempts, and experimental results across long-running research sessions. GPT-5.6 Sol was the primary reasoning engine. We directed the investigation, challenged its findings, and validated the interesting ones against actual kernel behavior on systems we controlled," Paulos Yibelo told The Hacker News. Vercel said no report in the challenge showed anyone reading a customer's files, secrets, or application data. items.summary: Threat actors are exploiting a critical command execution flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-110447, in the Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode) for Nextcloud. [...]
items.articleText: Hackers exploit Collabora RCE flaw to backdoor Nextcloud servers By Bill Toulas October 15, 2026 04:25 PM 0 Threat actors are exploiting a critical command execution flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-110447, in the Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode) for Nextcloud. Multiple administrator reports indicate that attacks began in mid-September, roughly a month before the formal security bulletin , the GitHub advisory , and CVE publication . CVE-2026-110447 impacts richdocumentscode versions before 26.4.303 and resides in the Nextcloud app’s mechanism for starting the bundled Collabora server. The flaw affects only the optional built-in CODE server app. Standalone Collabora Online servers, Docker and RPM/DEB installations, and Nextcloud All-in-One deployments remain unaffected, according to Collabora. The attacks involve sending a malicious request to the app’s proxy.php endpoint, triggering OS command injection. A key prerequisite for successful exploitation is that the built-in CODE server must be stopped (e.g., after a restart, upgrade, crash). Authentication or user interaction is not required. System administrators impacted by malicious activity reported attacks against multiple endpoints dating back to September 10. According to the reports, the attacker planted PHP webshells and used them to search for password databases, password manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets. Some users also reported that ransomware operators are exploiting the flaw , but BleepingComputer could not independently confirm this. System administrators are recommended to upgrade to version 26.4.303 or later, or remove the server app if not needed. The vendor warned that disabling the app is insufficient. Beyond the mid-September warnings from maintainers, a community warning was also published on October 3, urging administrators to update immediately due to ongoing exploitation. However, the lack of a CVE ID made it more difficult for administrators to pinpoint the issue correctly and implement efficient defenses. A study from cybersecurity company Second Security illustrates the gap between security fixes and formal vulnerability notifications. The firm analyzed real-world examples from open-source flaws and found that the median interval between public fixes and CVE publication was 39 days in August, up from 5.1 days in January. The researchers suggest that growing volumes of AI-assisted vulnerability discoveries are straining CVE processing and contributing to publication delays. items.articleText: Android gets AI defenses against messaging scams, fake calls By Bill Toulas October 15, 2026 03:48 PM 0 Google announced new AI-powered defenses against scam messages and call-forwarding abuse on Android, currently rolling out to eligible devices. The new measures aim to address the increased sophistication of scams targeting mobile users, including fraudulent bank alerts and voice-cloning attacks. “Mobile scams have evolved far beyond basic robocalls and phishing texts, turning into sophisticated operations that use spoofed numbers, fake bank alerts, and AI voice cloning,” Google says . “With scams growing harder to spot, it’s nearly impossible for users to catch every red flag themselves,” added the tech giant. Google says its existing Phone and Messages scam detection flags more than 5 million suspected scam calls and texts monthly, but the new measures are expected to catch even more threats. Cloud-based scam analysis The new protections focus on Google Messages and rely on cloud-based Gemini-backed analysis for complex conversations, scrutinizing them for signs of fraud. The system analyzes conversations with unknown senders within the encrypted Private AI Compute environment, protecting user privacy at all times. The new mode also adds on-device Gemini Nano (local AI model) checks for unfamiliar links using real-time web signals, plus clearer warnings before opening links from unsaved numbers. The new cloud-based protections are currently disabled by default, allowing users to activate them. Scam alert on Messages Source: Google Other improvements Apart from the Google Messages protection, Google has also implemented the enhancements in other areas of the Android system: On-device scam detection in chat notifications, previously launched on Pixel , will reach hundreds of millions more users through Android device partners later this year. Android’s existing sensitive-information masking is now expanding to Chrome and Android WebView, hiding login fields and payment screens during live screen sharing. Android blocks apps from silently enabling call forwarding in the background and warns users before manually entered MMI forwarding codes take effect. Call forwarding warning Source: Google Google is also expanding its verified bank calls system, introduced earlier this year , adding financial institutions from more. This system checks whether a real bank’s call center initiated an incoming call or if it is a spoofing attempt. If the verification fails, the call is automatically ended. items.summary: A proxyjacking campaign has impacted devices in 34 countries, monetizing victims' internet connections through a commercial residential proxy network. [...]
items.articleText: Hackers hijack D-Link, Ubiquiti devices to resell your stolen bandwidth By Bill Toulas October 15, 2026 02:20 PM 0 A proxyjacking campaign has impacted devices in 34 countries, monetizing victims’ internet connections through a commercial residential proxy network. The operator installed Pawns.app, a legitimate bandwidth-sharing application that lets users earn money by sharing their internet connections, on devices without the owners’ consent. Pawns.app account holders are rewarded for allowing traffic from other users to flow through their network, provided it runs on trusted, non-blocking IP addresses. By installing the app on multiple systems, the attacker likely accumulated larger payouts. Source: GreyNoise Threat intelligence company GreyNoise discovered the campaign while investigating suspicious activity at an unnamed organization, and identified at least 143 compromised devices worldwide. According to the researchers, the attacker leveraged several vulnerabilities to breach edge devices and install the Pawns.app software: CVE-2024-3272 and CVE-2024-3273 in D-Link ShareCenter NAS CVE-2021-44228 in Ubiquiti UniFi Video NVR CVE-2025-31324 in SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer The researchers also observed targeting of Hikvision and Dahua DVR/NVR devices, but did not specify the vulnerabilities exploited in these systems. GreyNoise says that, in some cases, the attackers configured SSH key authentication as a backup access method. Configuring SSH access Source: GreyNoise Even legitimate proxy networks can route suspicious traffic through volunteer-operated nodes due to insufficient oversight, potentially resulting in IP address blocks for participating users or exposing them to allegations of involvement in illegal activities. The FBI previously warned about such networks being used to carry out large-scale credential stuffing attacks against online platforms. GreyNoise provides a free service (account required) for users to check if their IP address is part of a known legitimate or “gray” proxying service. It is generally advisable to avoid downloading software from untrusted sources, as purportedly free software may contain malware that enrolls devices in residential proxy networks. Threat actors also commonly exploit known vulnerabilities in internet-connected devices. Keeping NAS devices, video recorders, and other internet-facing systems updated can significantly reduce the risk of compromise.
